subtitle: Whatever your job, you have a role in equity. Learn to connect it to your own work, contribute useful evidence and act within your responsibilities.
scope: For employees in any DHS program, service line or business area. The course develops practical contributions from individual roles without assuming everyone controls policy, budgets or personnel decisions. Practice cases use no real service or employee records. Learning practice does not replace required equity analysis, assigned training or formal reporting procedures.
introTranscript: Equity work is part of how DHS makes decisions, communicates, uses resources and delivers services. You can contribute whether your work involves people directly or supports the systems they use. Your contribution might be identifying an unclear instruction, checking a comparison, examining a handoff or preparing a supported question for the responsible decision maker. This course follows a team in this example preparing a service information session. You will identify your part in the work, examine a possible barrier, consider different perspectives, communicate a useful recommendation and plan follow-through. You do not need to promise a change outside your authority or make an unsupported finding. Work at your own pace and use a practice example or a suitable draft for practice.

lessons.title: Find the decision in your own task
lessons.summary: Identify one point where your work affects another person’s opportunity to participate.
lessons.objective: Identify a decision or handoff within a practice job task.
objectives: Identify a decision or handoff within a practice job task.
Describe who may be affected by that task.
Distinguish your contribution from a decision outside your authority.
takeaways: Equity considerations apply across DHS work.
A concrete task is a useful starting point for inquiry.
Contributing a concern does not require control over every decision.
lessons.statement: Start with a task you can describe and the people it may affect.

image.caption: Four colleagues talk in a bright office hallway while holding laptops and folders.

intro.heading: Your role is a practical starting point
intro.body:
DHS’s Equity Policy expects employees to apply an equity lens to their daily work as well as to policies, practices, budgets and other decisions. That expectation is relevant to a service worker, an analyst, an administrative employee and a person supporting finance or technology. Their responsibilities differ, but each can examine the effects of the work they actually perform.

Consider a team in this example preparing a service information session. One employee drafts the invitation, another arranges the room, a third checks the participant response process and a fourth prepares an internal summary. Each task includes decisions. The invitation explains who can attend and how to respond. The room arrangements affect participation. The response process determines what information people must provide. The summary can influence what the team believes happened.

Choose one task rather than claiming responsibility for the entire program. Describe its purpose, your part and the next handoff. Then identify who may be affected. You may have permission to propose an invitation revision but not to change eligibility, authorize spending or release information. Naming that boundary helps the team connect a useful contribution to the correct decision maker. It does not excuse ignoring a concern that needs to be raised through the appropriate process.

A useful starting question is specific: does this invitation explain an available response route clearly? A broader question, such as whether the entire service is equitable, may require additional evidence and expertise. Begin with the question the task supports and widen it responsibly if the inquiry shows a relevant connection. Use the practice case in this course so practice does not disclose protected information or imply that a real person has failed in their work.

inThisLesson: Describe your contribution and its limits.
lessons.keyStatement: A specific contribution can inform a larger decision without replacing it.

flashcards.back: A concrete part of the work with a purpose, action and result.
A choice that can affect how work is carried out or used.
A transfer of information or responsibility to the next step.
The difference between what you may decide and what belongs to another authorized role.

items.title: Purpose
items.body: State what the practice session is intended to help people do. An invitation can be clear about attendance while unclear about the response route. Knowing the purpose helps identify which question belongs in the review and avoids expanding the inquiry without a reason.

items.title: People affected
items.body: Consider people using the information and staff carrying out the task. Do not assume a single colleague speaks for everyone. Identify the perspectives relevant to this decision and what you still need to learn through an appropriate process.

items.title: Responsibility
items.body: Your role might be drafting, checking or carrying out a choice made elsewhere. Describe that accurately. You can prepare a concern, recommend a revision and ask who owns the decision without claiming the power to waive a rule or promise a service change.

tabs.label: Administrative work
tabs.body: The employee arranging the session can check whether the published invitation matches the arrangements and whether an identified participation question reached the responsible person. This supports the task without making an accommodation or eligibility determination on the employee’s own authority.

tabs.label: Program work
tabs.body: A program employee can clarify the service purpose and applicable requirements. Their knowledge helps distinguish a necessary condition from an unclear instruction. Changes still follow the authority and procedures assigned to that role.

tabs.label: Analysis work
tabs.body: An analyst can identify what the response records measure and which comparison is suitable. A precise total does not settle whether everyone had a usable opportunity. The analyst’s contribution should show the evidence and its limitations.

check.question: Which starting point fits the practice invitation task?
check.correct: Identify the response instruction, who uses it and who can authorize a revision.
wrong: Declare the whole agency equitable because the invitation was sent.
Change eligibility to remove every possible difficulty.
Wait until you control the entire service before raising a question.
check.feedbackCorrect: This connects a manageable task to affected people and the appropriate decision responsibility.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A sent invitation does not establish an equitable outcome, and a drafting role does not authorize eligibility changes. Staff can contribute useful questions while respecting the decisions assigned elsewhere.

items.text: The employee drafts the session invitation.
The analyst summarizes the recorded responses.
Ask whether the response instruction matches the available route.
Identify who can approve a supported revision.
Promise an eligibility exception without authority.
Commit funds because a learning activity suggested an idea.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: You prepare the invitation and notice that the response route is not explained. You do not control the service rules.
options: Identify the missing instruction and ask the responsible person to review an accurate revision.
Rewrite the rules yourself and announce an exception.
Conclude you have no equity role because someone else controls the rules.
responses: This addresses the specific task while preserving decision authority.
A concern does not authorize changing the service rules.
Your drafting role can identify a barrier question and prepare a useful recommendation.

lessons.transfer: Describe a practice task, one decision point, affected people and the responsibility you hold.

move.control: You can describe your contribution without claiming the entire decision.
move.failure: The concern stays vague or leads to an unauthorized promise.
move.next: Choose a practice task and name the relevant handoff.

lessons.title: Turn a concern into a supported question
lessons.summary: Separate an observation, a possible explanation and the evidence needed next.
lessons.objective: Write a question tied to an observable task.
objectives: Write a question tied to an observable task.
Separate evidence from a possible explanation.
Identify a suitable next source without collecting unnecessary personal information.
takeaways: A concern becomes more useful when its basis is clear.
A possible explanation is not an established cause.
Use evidence that fits the question and the information rules.
lessons.statement: Describe what you know, what you think may be happening and what you need to check.

image.caption: Four colleagues talk in a bright office hallway while holding laptops and folders.

intro.heading: A question can invite inquiry without making a finding
intro.body:
An equity concern does not need to arrive as a proven conclusion. It needs enough detail for the responsible people to understand what should be examined. Distinguish what you observed from what you believe may explain it. This makes the concern more useful and leaves room for evidence that changes the initial interpretation.

In the practice case, the invitation directs people to a response form but does not explain an available assisted route. That is a document observation. You think some people may miss the session because they cannot use the published route. That is a possible explanation. The invitation alone does not show who missed the session, why they did not respond or whether the assisted route was effective. A useful question is whether the response instructions and available support provide a usable opportunity to respond.

Choose the next evidence source for that question. The current invitation, the authorized response instructions and feedback gathered through a suitable engagement process may help. An unrelated employee file or a collection of individual service records is not automatically justified because the inquiry concerns equity. Follow the applicable information rules and involve the people authorized to decide what data may be used and shared. Removing names alone does not establish that a record is safe to disclose.

Record the limit as part of the contribution. You can say that the instruction omits the assisted route and recommend checking its practical use. Avoid claiming that the omission caused every nonresponse or that a group’s identity explains its behavior. Clear uncertainty strengthens a responsible inquiry. It also helps the team decide whether the first question is ready for action, needs further evidence or belongs in a broader authorized review.

lessons.keyStatement: A clear question supports investigation; it does not supply its conclusion.

flashcards.back: Something supported by the material or information you actually examined.
A proposed account of what may be happening that needs examination.
Relevant information that is missing or insufficient for the claim.
A conclusion stated at the strength the evidence supports.

accordion.heading: Prepare a question people can use

items.title: Specific wording
items.body: The invitation does not describe the assisted response route is more useful than the team does not care about access. The first identifies a checkable feature. The second assigns motive that the document does not establish and can distract from the practical question.

items.title: Relevant information
items.body: Ask which material could answer the question before collecting it. A process instruction may explain the route, while authorized aggregate information may describe use. Neither automatically explains each person’s reason or gives permission to circulate protected records.

items.title: Changing your interpretation
items.body: An inquiry may show the assisted route is well explained elsewhere, or that people encounter a different barrier. Update the concern rather than protecting the initial explanation. The goal is a supported understanding that can guide action.

tabs.label: Too broad
tabs.body: Everyone is being excluded does not tell the team which evidence supports the statement or what can be checked. A broad concern may need attention, but the note should describe its basis and avoid asserting facts that have not been established.

tabs.label: Supported question
tabs.body: The published invitation omits the assisted route; can we review whether people can find and use it? This identifies the material, possible access issue and next inquiry without claiming the omission explains every response.

tabs.label: Missing information
tabs.body: We do not yet know how people used the assisted route is an honest limit. Do not replace it with no one needed help or the route failed for everyone. Both would turn missing evidence into an unsupported conclusion.

check.question: What can the practice invitation establish by itself?
check.correct: It omits the assisted response instruction, while effects and reasons need further evidence.
wrong: Everyone who did not respond was excluded by that omission.
The staff member intended to make access difficult.
No listed complaint means the route worked for everyone.
check.feedbackCorrect: The document supports an observation about its contents, not a complete account of participation or motive.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Nonresponse, intent and success cannot be established from the instruction alone. Use relevant authorized information, affected perspectives and a bounded question to examine possible effects.

items.text: The practice invitation lists only the form route.
The assisted route is described in a separate instruction.
People may not find the route when instructions are separated.
The unfamiliar term may affect how people respond.
Compare the invitation with the authorized process instruction.
Seek suitable feedback about finding and using the response routes.

lessons.next: Next, consider whose knowledge can improve the inquiry.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A colleague calls lower response a lack of interest without examining the invitation or asking about the task.
options: Ask what evidence supports that explanation and propose examining the instructions and appropriate feedback.
Declare that every nonresponse proves an access failure.
Use the group label as a substitute for asking about the task.
responses: This keeps the inquiry specific and open to evidence.
The opposite causal claim is still unsupported.
A group label cannot explain an individual response or replace process evidence.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice concern in three parts: observation, possible explanation and next evidence question.

move.control: You can make a checkable contribution and state uncertainty.
move.failure: An assumption about cause or motive is presented as a fact.
move.next: Review the practice invitation and write a bounded question.

lessons.title: Bring relevant perspectives into the work
lessons.summary: Plan a useful contribution process without asking people to represent an entire group.
lessons.objective: Identify knowledge relevant to the practice decision.
objectives: Identify knowledge relevant to the practice decision.
Describe a participation choice that can inform the review.
Explain how input may support a changed or unchanged choice.
takeaways: Affected people can contribute knowledge the team does not hold.
Participation should relate to a real question and decision.
One person’s input does not represent an entire community.
lessons.statement: Ask for relevant experience while the decision can still be informed.

image.caption: Four colleagues talk in a bright office hallway while holding laptops and folders.

intro.heading: Make participation useful and accurate
intro.body:
People who carry out a task and people who use it may know different parts of the process. Staff understand the service purpose and operational responsibilities. People responding to an invitation may know which instruction is unclear or which step creates difficulty. Neither perspective automatically supplies the whole account. A useful review connects these kinds of knowledge to a question the team can act on.

In the practice case, the team wants to learn whether people can find and use the session response routes. An appropriate engagement process can ask about that task instead of demanding personal histories unrelated to the decision. Explain the purpose, what choices are open, how information will be handled and any limits on the process. Do not promise confidentiality, influence or a service change beyond what the authorized process can provide. Use approved procedures for actual engagement and information handling.

Avoid treating a colleague or participant as the spokesperson for a category of people. Someone can describe their own experience without knowing every perspective within a community. Relevant differences may call for additional input, appropriate language or communication support and different opportunities to contribute. The review should not require someone to disclose an identity or explain a painful experience to earn a voice.

After the input is considered, explain how it informed the choice. It may support a revision, clarify an implementation condition or support keeping a requirement with a clearer explanation. Input does not have to produce a change to be meaningful, but collecting it after the choice is closed and pretending the decision remains open misrepresents its purpose. Be accurate about influence. If your role is preparing the invitation, you can recommend a participation question and identify who should arrange the proper process.

inThisLesson: Explain how input informed the choice.
lessons.keyStatement: Participation is useful when its purpose and influence are clear.

flashcards.back: Knowledge from someone whose participation or experience may be shaped by the work.
A decision that can still be informed by relevant evidence or input.
The boundary of what one person’s experience can tell the team.
An account of how input was considered and what happens next.

items.title: A real question
items.body: Ask how people find and use the response instruction. This is more focused than asking whether they approve of the entire agency. A narrow question can still reveal a relevant broader concern, which should be referred or examined through the appropriate process.

items.title: Accurate influence
items.body: If a service rule is fixed for this review, say so and identify which communication or implementation choices remain open. Do not imply participants can change eligibility when that is outside the process. Accurate limits allow people to decide how to contribute.

items.title: A usable route
items.body: Consider whether the invitation and participation method fit the task and the people involved. A meeting is one possible route, not a universal solution. Use applicable access requirements and appropriate support rather than asking staff to improvise a legally required service.

tabs.label: Single spokesperson
tabs.body: Asking one person to speak for everyone may hide differences within a group and impose an unfair expectation. Invite their actual knowledge and examine whether additional perspectives are relevant to the decision.

tabs.label: Focused contribution
tabs.body: A suitable task-based question lets people describe a step they used without requiring unrelated personal details. The team can compare this input with process information and state where knowledge remains limited.

tabs.label: Feedback after review
tabs.body: Explain how input shaped the decision and which issues remain open. An unchanged requirement can be explained with reasons and appropriate next steps. Avoid reporting a change that did not occur or implying agreement from everyone who participated.

check.question: Which invitation to contribute is most useful in the practice review?
check.correct: Explain the response-route question, the open choices and how input will be considered.
wrong: Ask one colleague to represent all people with similar backgrounds.
Invite input after the final decision while saying every choice remains open.
Require unrelated personal disclosures to demonstrate commitment.
check.feedbackCorrect: This helps people decide how to contribute and connects their knowledge to a real review.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A single person cannot supply every group perspective. Participation should be truthful about influence and should not demand unrelated disclosures. Use the actual engagement and information procedures for real work.

sorting.heading: Relevant inquiry, accurate limit or misleading participation?

items.text: Ask which response instruction was difficult to find.
Seek knowledge about the task from people who use it.
Explain that eligibility is outside this invitation review.
State that one participant’s experience does not represent everyone.
Call the decision open after it has already been finalized.
Report unanimous agreement because several people attended.

lessons.next: Next, compare a practical improvement with its responsibilities and effects.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Participants say the two response routes are easier to understand when explained together. One service requirement remains unchanged.
options: How the feedback informed the instruction revision and why the requirement remains, with any appropriate next review.
That participants controlled every service decision.
That unchanged requirements prove the feedback had no value.
responses: This gives an accurate account of influence, reasons and remaining questions.
The team should not promise or report authority participants did not have.
Input can inform implementation and the reasons for an unchanged choice.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice participation question, its influence limit and a follow-through statement.

move.control: You can connect relevant knowledge to a truthful review process.
move.failure: Attendance substitutes for evidence that input was useful or representative.
move.next: Plan a task-based practice question and explain what can be influenced.

lessons.title: Prepare a recommendation within your responsibility
lessons.summary: Compare an improvement’s benefits, burdens and decision requirements.
objectives: Identify who may carry each option’s work or cost.
Prepare a recommendation that preserves authority and uncertainty.
takeaways: An improvement may shift work as well as reduce a barrier.
A recommendation needs reasons, limits and the correct decision responsibility.
Supporting an idea does not authorize changing a rule or committing resources.
lessons.statement: Recommend a supported next step and explain what it requires.

image.caption: Four colleagues talk in a bright office hallway while holding laptops and folders.

intro.heading: Practical action includes the work needed to carry it out
intro.body:
A practical recommendation explains more than what would look better. It connects the identified concern to an option, the evidence supporting it, the people who would carry out the work and the responsibilities that govern the decision. This helps a responsible decision maker consider the proposal without mistaking a course exercise for permission to act.

In the practice session case, one option is to explain both response routes in the invitation. Another is to add a staffed response appointment. The first may clarify existing information; the second may provide useful assistance but require scheduling, staff time and a decision about resources. Neither option is automatically best for every person. Compare how each addresses the specific task and what remains unresolved. An instruction revision may still need appropriate communication and access review before release.

Describe who may carry the burden. Participants might need an additional appointment, staff might need preparation time and another office might need to support the route. A suggestion that helps one step but creates an inaccessible or unsupported step elsewhere needs further thought. Do not assume an office has capacity or authority because the team favors the idea. Ask the people responsible for the work and use the applicable decision process.

Your contribution can be a recommendation rather than a final authorization. State the proposed next step, its reasons, any evidence gap and the role that should review it. Keep eligibility, spending, contracts and protected information within their authorized procedures. If the proposed action falls under the DHS Equity Policy’s formal-analysis requirement, the responsible staff still need to use the required process. This course’s comparison helps prepare a useful contribution; it does not replace that analysis or certify that the outcome will be equitable.

lessons.keyStatement: A useful recommendation explains both its reasons and its implementation needs.

flashcards.back: A possible response to the identified task or concern.
Work, information, resources or authorization required to carry out an option.
Time, effort or other demands the option places on affected people or staff.
A supported proposed next step for the responsible decision process.

items.title: Connection to the concern
items.body: Explain how showing both response routes addresses the missing instruction. Do not claim it will resolve every service barrier. A recommendation should keep the link between the specific problem and the proposed action visible.

items.title: Resource question
items.body: A staffed appointment requires more than adding a sentence. Identify staffing, scheduling and any approval needed before it is promised. Asking the responsible office about feasibility is part of the work, not a reason to dismiss access needs without consideration.

items.title: Evidence limit
items.body: If feedback supports clearer instructions but appointment demand is unknown, state that distinction. The team can recommend the supported instruction review and a suitable next question about assistance. A confident recommendation does not need invented certainty.

tabs.label: Clarify existing routes
tabs.body: This option addresses information that is already available but separated. Check that the revised wording is accurate, understandable and appropriately reviewed. It may reduce one barrier while leaving other participation needs to be addressed.

tabs.label: Add an appointment
tabs.body: This option could offer assistance but also add an extra step and staff workload. Consider who can use it, whether the timing is practical and who can authorize and provide it. Do not promise a service that has not been arranged.

tabs.label: Keep and explain
tabs.body: An unchanged option may be supported by evidence or applicable requirements. Explain the reason and remaining concern rather than calling it equitable simply because it is familiar. Identify what would justify a further review.

check.question: What should accompany a recommendation for a staffed response appointment?
check.correct: Its connection to the concern, expected work and access needs, evidence limits and responsible authorization.
wrong: A promise that it will remove every inequity.
A statement that any employee may commit the staffing.
A requirement that every participant use the appointment regardless of the applicable process.
check.feedbackCorrect: This allows the responsible people to assess the option and its practical conditions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A recommendation cannot guarantee all outcomes or create spending, service or participation authority. Explain the option’s actual purpose and requirements, preserve available choices under the applicable process and state uncertainties.

sorting.heading: Reason, implementation need or unsupported promise?

items.text: The practice feedback supports explaining the routes together.
The proposed revision addresses a missing instruction.
The responsible office needs to review staffing and timing.
The instruction needs accurate access and communication review.
Every inequity will disappear after this revision.
The employee can authorize a new service without assigned authority.

lessons.next: Next, distinguish practical guidance from procedures that must be followed.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Your draft suggests an appointment route, but staffing and authority have not been reviewed.
options: As an option with reasons, unresolved conditions and a request for the responsible decision review.
As an announced service starting tomorrow.
As proof that a formal equity analysis is complete.
responses: This preserves the idea while stating what must be resolved before implementation.
An unsupported promise can mislead people and create work the team has not arranged.
An option comparison in this course does not complete the required analysis process.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice recommendation with its reason, burden, uncertainty and decision responsibility.

move.control: You can recommend action without promising authority or outcomes you do not hold.
move.failure: An attractive idea becomes an unsupported service commitment.
move.next: Compare the two practice options and identify the next responsible review.

lessons.title: Use guidance and formal processes for their proper purposes
lessons.summary: Keep learning support, required analysis and reporting responsibilities distinct.
lessons.objective: Distinguish optional consultant guidance from an applicable formal procedure.
objectives: Distinguish optional consultant guidance from an applicable formal procedure.
Identify a formal-analysis requirement described in the DHS Equity Policy.
Recognize different employee and manager reporting responsibilities under Policy 1436.
takeaways: Consultant support helps staff develop their own equity work.
Required analysis and reporting retain their actual roles and procedures.
A learning conversation should not delay an applicable duty.
lessons.statement: Use support to strengthen your work and the appropriate process when it is required.

image.caption: Four colleagues talk in a bright office hallway while holding laptops and folders.

intro.heading: Support and responsibility work together
intro.body:
The One DSD program is led by the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant. The consultant can provide guidance, knowledge and feedback that help staff develop their own capability. Staff across DHS can use the learning resources without a universal requirement to send every question or draft through the consultant. This support does not replace other roles established by agency policy.

The DHS Equity Policy requires formal analysis for actions with prolonged or long-term impact scheduled for approval by specified leadership roles. Those actions must be accompanied by the DHS Equity Analysis or Equity Scan within the toolkit, or a customized tool developed in consultation with an equity director for the business area. The policy also sets broader employee expectations concerning toolkit use and learning. The short practice in this course does not satisfy all of those requirements or establish approved training credit.

A workplace report has a different purpose from a request for general feedback on an invitation. Under MMB Policy 1436, employees are strongly encouraged to report protected-class harassment or discrimination through the listed reporting options. Managers and supervisors have an immediate duty to report allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer, and must follow agency complaint and investigation procedures. Do not turn optional consultation into a prerequisite or a reason to delay an applicable responsibility. Authorized investigation duties remain with the assigned roles and procedures.

You do not need to decide every policy question yourself before using a proper route. Describe the concern accurately and provide relevant information through the appropriate process. Ask for guidance when its purpose is learning or analysis support. When an applicable procedure governs the issue, follow it and preserve its role responsibilities. The practice course case is practice in recognizing the distinction, not a legal finding about a real incident.

lessons.keyStatement: Optional support does not replace an applicable analysis or reporting procedure.

flashcards.back: Support that develops staff capability through knowledge, questions and feedback.
The required policy process for covered actions, using the specified toolkit or appropriately developed customized tool.
A duty or reporting option established by the applicable policy and the person’s role.
The agency process and authorized responsibilities governing the actual issue.

accordion.heading: Choose the process by its purpose

items.title: A learning question
items.body: A staff member can ask the consultant how to examine an invitation’s possible barrier or improve a supported note. That assistance should build the staff member’s capability. It does not turn every everyday draft into a mandatory consultant approval process.

items.title: A covered action
items.body: When the actual proposal has the impact and approval conditions described by the Equity Policy, use its required analysis process. A completed course comparison or a general consultant discussion cannot be substituted for the policy’s specified toolkit and roles.

items.title: A workplace allegation
items.body: Use Policy 1436’s reporting options and role requirements for a protected-class concern. Managers and supervisors must immediately report allegations or incidents to HR or the agency AAO. Do not require a consultant appointment or informal resolution first; authorized investigations follow agency procedures.

tabs.label: Developing skill
tabs.body: Guidance can help you frame a question, examine assumptions and improve your work. Staff retain responsibility for their contributions. The consultant does not need to perform every task for them or become a universal permission gate.

tabs.label: Meeting a requirement
tabs.body: Check the applicable policy, assigned role and procedure rather than relying on a course label. The Equity Policy’s required analysis and training arrangements are distinct from this learning activity. Seek the proper business-area guidance for actual work.

tabs.label: Making a report
tabs.body: A report about alleged protected-class conduct is not just another worksheet scenario. Use the listed routes, do not retaliate and preserve required responsibilities. This course does not adjudicate the allegation or authorize an improvised investigation outside assigned procedures.

check.question: A supervisor receives an allegation of protected-class harassment. Which response fits Policy 1436?
check.correct: Immediately report it to HR or the agency AAO and follow agency procedures, without waiting for optional consultant guidance.
wrong: Hold it until the next learning session.
Require the reporter to first complete an equity worksheet.
Treat a supportive conversation as the completed investigation.
check.feedbackCorrect: The policy gives managers and supervisors a distinct immediate reporting duty and requires the agency’s procedures.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A learning or consultation process cannot delay the supervisor’s reporting duty or replace an authorized investigation. Employees’ reporting options and supervisors’ responsibilities differ; preserve the appropriate role and process.

sorting.heading: Learning support, required analysis or reporting process?

items.text: Ask for feedback on a practice equity question.
Use a resource to improve your option comparison.
Use the specified toolkit for an actual covered long-term action.
Recognize that a customized tool must follow the policy’s equity-director consultation condition.
A supervisor immediately reports a protected-class allegation to HR or the AAO.
An employee uses a listed reporting option for a protected-class concern.

lessons.next: Next, plan a contribution that can be reviewed and improved.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A staff member asks whether every invitation draft needs consultant approval, while the team prepares a separate covered long-term proposal.
options: Optional guidance can support the invitation work; the covered proposal still needs the policy’s required analysis process.
The consultant must approve every routine draft before staff can work.
A finished learning course automatically completes the covered proposal’s required analysis.
responses: This supports independent staff capability while preserving the actual formal requirement.
The program does not create a universal consultant permission gate.
Learning practice does not replace the specified policy process or establish required training credit.

lessons.transfer: For a practice situation, state whether you need learning support, an applicable formal process or both, and why.

move.control: You can use support without replacing required responsibilities.
move.failure: An optional conversation becomes a delay or a substitute for the proper process.

lessons.title: Follow through on a responsible contribution
lessons.summary: Record the action, decision responsibility and evidence needed to review its effect.
lessons.objective: Prepare a concise contribution note for a practice task.
objectives: Prepare a concise contribution note for a practice task.
Distinguish completing an action from achieving an intended result.
Identify a suitable review question and remaining uncertainty.
takeaways: Follow-through makes a contribution usable beyond the first conversation.
Completing a task does not establish its effect for everyone.
Review can lead to a changed or unchanged choice with reasons.
lessons.statement: Make the next action and the question for review clear.

image.caption: Four colleagues talk in a bright office hallway while holding laptops and folders.

intro.heading: A useful contribution includes what happens afterward
intro.body:
A contribution is easier to use when the team can see what was proposed, who is responsible for the next step and how the result will be reviewed. This does not require a large report for every routine task. It requires enough information to preserve the question, the reasons and the responsibility without overstating what has been decided.

For the practice session, a short note can describe the invitation’s missing response instruction, the relevant feedback, an accurately reviewed wording option and the person responsible for release. It can also identify a review question: could participants find and use the response routes? If an appointment option still needs staffing review, keep that condition visible instead of presenting it as an available service. Record unresolved matters through the appropriate work process.

Distinguish action from result. Publishing a revised invitation shows that the revision was made. It does not by itself show that everyone received it, understood it or had a usable response opportunity. Relevant authorized feedback or suitable process information may help examine those questions. A comparison should have consistent definitions and appropriate information protections. A change over time does not automatically establish that the wording alone caused the result.

Review should be proportionate to the task and carried out within the relevant responsibilities. It may support keeping the revision, changing another instruction or referring a broader concern. Explain the evidence and the reason for the decision, including an unchanged choice. The consultant can help staff interpret the work and develop their skill while staff retain their tasks. For this learning activity, use the practice session or a suitable draft; you do not need to change a real service, obtain a live outcome or disclose actual records to complete the practice.

lessons.keyStatement: Follow-through preserves the question, responsibility and evidence limit.

flashcards.back: A concise account of the concern, evidence, proposed step and relevant limits.
Information showing a task was carried out, such as a reviewed revision being released.
A question about what the action helped people do or experience.
A reasoned choice to keep, change or refer the work based on appropriate evidence.

items.title: Enough context
items.body: State the practice task, the instruction concern and the supported proposal. A reader should understand why the note matters without needing your entire conversation. Include relevant limits and keep protected information in the proper process.

items.title: Named responsibility
items.body: Identify the assigned role or person responsible for the next step, without inventing their agreement. If ownership is unresolved, say it needs clarification. The course exercise cannot assign work, commit resources or create formal authority by itself.

items.title: Review with reasons
items.body: State what would help examine the route’s use and what the evidence cannot establish. If the choice stays unchanged, explain how input and requirements informed that decision. Do not demand a change merely to prove the exercise was completed.

tabs.label: Revision released
tabs.body: This shows an implementation step occurred. Check whether the version and available route match the intended action. It is useful evidence, but it cannot substitute for information about understanding or participation.

tabs.label: Task feedback
tabs.body: Appropriate feedback about finding and using the route can illuminate the result question. Explain how it was obtained and its limits. Do not treat several responses as the experiences of everyone or infer motives from nonresponse.

tabs.label: Further inquiry
tabs.body: If feedback identifies another relevant difficulty, identify a suitable next responsibility and inquiry. The team may need a broader authorized analysis. An unresolved question is not proof of success, failure or personal blame.

check.question: What does releasing the revised practice invitation establish?
check.correct: The revision was implemented; its effects on finding and using the routes still need appropriate review.
wrong: Every participant had an equitable outcome.
The wording caused every later response.
All formal policy obligations are complete.
check.feedbackCorrect: This separates the completed task from its intended effect and the requirements that remain.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Implementation evidence is useful but does not prove universal access, causation or full compliance. Match the review question to relevant evidence, preserve authority and state what remains unknown.

sorting.heading: Action evidence, result inquiry or overclaim?

items.text: The reviewed invitation now explains the two available routes.
The responsible role released the approved revision.
Could people find and use the response routes?
What suitable feedback identifies a remaining difficulty?
A completed course proves the service is equitable for everyone.
A later response increase proves the wording was the sole cause.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to prepare a practice contribution or improve a suitable draft at your own pace.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The revised invitation was released, and the team has not yet reviewed its use. A summary calls every barrier resolved.
options: The revision was made; the team still needs appropriate evidence about use and remaining concerns.
All barriers are resolved because the new wording is clearer.
No progress occurred because every result is not yet known.
responses: This records real implementation progress and the honest limit on its effects.
Clearer wording is not proof of universal access or resolution.
An implementation step can be valuable while result questions remain open.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a practice note with the task, evidence, proposed action, responsible next step and result question.

move.control: You can contribute to equity work with evidence, responsibility and follow-through.
move.failure: A completed activity becomes a claim of universal success or compliance.
move.next: Use the practice case or a suitable draft to practice; do not disclose actual protected records.

jobAid.subtitle: A practical contribution from your role
remember: You can contribute useful equity work within your role, seek guidance and follow the formal processes that apply. A learning exercise does not complete every policy requirement.

sections.heading: Start with the task
items: What does the work help someone do?
Which choice or handoff is within your responsibility?
Who may be affected, and who holds the next decision authority?

sections.heading: Prepare a supported question
items: State the observation separately from a possible explanation.
Identify relevant evidence and affected perspectives through an appropriate process.
Keep information use and sharing within applicable rules; removing names alone does not establish safety.

sections.heading: Compare and recommend
items: Explain how an option addresses the concern and what remains unresolved.
Identify work, access needs, resources and authorization before promising implementation.
Make the reasons, uncertainty and next responsible review clear.

sections.heading: Use the proper process
items: Optional consultant guidance helps staff develop their capability; it is not a universal permission gate.
Covered actions still require the Equity Policy’s specified analysis process and roles.
Follow applicable reporting duties and agency procedures without waiting for optional learning support.

sections.heading: Follow through
items: Distinguish the action completed from the result you want to examine.
Explain how input informed the choice, including unchanged choices and reasons.
Use a practice case or suitable draft for practice; this course does not certify compliance, training credit or a real outcome.

sources.title: DHS — Equity Policy
sources.note: Daily equity-lens expectations, roles and required analysis for covered actions. The learning exercises prepare staff to contribute; they do not complete the agency’s required process.

sources.title: MMB — Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited, Policy 1436
sources.note: Employee reporting options, distinct manager and supervisor responsibilities, non-retaliation and agency investigation procedures. This course does not decide whether a particular incident violates the policy.
